segment:
He wasn’t upset. He had said so himself, and she trusted him. But the air seemed too thick, like smoke or fog. Her lungs could not find room for Jonah’s breaths. Her stomach was clenched tight, her skin too hot. She kept a little behind, watching his back, listening to the slow beat of his pulse.
What was wrong?
Jonah didn’t notice. He breathed through his mouth, in and out, and didn’t speed up his stride. Mara slowed hers to keep the same distance behind him. The street was still and quiet, a row of dim, unmarked windows behind which people slept.
Mara’s heart continued to beat, hard and fast, and she felt her lungs ache. She didn’t have words for what was wrong.
He started up a side street. His shoulders rose and fell with each breath. His hands stayed quiet at his sides, swinging very slowly. He slowed without looking back, waited for her.
Jonah didn’t offer comfort. He didn’t touch her. He stood beside her in silence. He didn’t expect anything, so she stopped thinking about what she could give him. She stopped trying to analyze her own reactions: whether they were normal; whether he was responsible for them. She let herself look up at the empty windows, the darkening sky.
He took a long, quiet breath.
She let out her own breath, slow.
He exhaled through his nose and tilted his head back, looking at the sky.
She let out another small breath, then one more. Her lungs were empty and aching again; she felt faint. She was shivering too.
Jonah didn’t speak or touch her, but he stayed by her side. She relaxed her shoulders, straightened up, and stepped closer.
She could see the sky: distant clouds, a few stars, a low-lying moon. Jonah had said something about it when they first came outside, though she hadn’t heard him at all. She hadn’t noticed anything except the cold and the empty sidewalk and the strange, silent house.
She turned to face Jonah again and met his eyes. His pupils were wide in the dark; she couldn’t see his irises or the color of his eyes. He watched her breathe: he was waiting.
The first thing she felt was the heat from his skin. He wore a long, dark coat over a thin gray shirt, which was open at his neck. She saw the smooth skin of his chest, exposed to the night air. His chest was warm. His cheeks were flushed from the cold, but his lips were still cool, and she felt her own pulse in her temples as he looked down at her.
Mara stepped closer. Her lips were dry; her heart beat faster with every breath.
She moved closer still. Her hands found his shoulders. Her left hand held tight to him while she lifted her right hand to touch his face. The cold air moved through the darkness, and Mara’s breath quickened again as he tilted his head toward her.
text:
They started at Fulcrum’s front steps, an instant after the last of the lab staff had gone indoors and locked up. Mara’s mouth felt raw and dry; her throat ached, and her shoulders were rigid and aching too. Her entire body was too hot despite the cold, and she didn’t feel the chill of the night air.
The others were gone. Jonah stood silently beside her, waiting. He was six inches taller than she was. He wasn’t looking at her; his head turned toward the empty drive, and he stared into the darkness beyond the lighted entrance. There was nothing there. She didn’t look. She watched him instead.
“I guess it’s time to go home.” Jonah’s voice was soft, almost inaudible. She had expected more after tonight: analysis or commiseration. Instead he turned sideways with a small sigh and started down the front steps. He swung both arms easily, as though he were on an ordinary walk, though it was the middle of the night and they were both on their way back to hotel rooms in a town she didn’t know.
She followed, trying to match his step. His dark hair rustled as he moved, a low whisper that went with the sound of his breathing: slow, even, no sign of anxiety.

segment:
The other participants had left immediately after the final debriefing. A group had been forming to go somewhere else; she knew from previous sessions that they would talk over drinks, or smoke, or eat something sweet to compensate for their hunger. She could have gone with them, but she hadn’t moved.
The drive was deserted. A few bright stars showed in the clear sky. He took long steps and swung his arms with each breath. The pavement was dry from a sunny afternoon. They walked down the driveway, side by side but without touching, out to the street. She wasn’t sure whether she should match his gait exactly or not. She matched his breathing instead, letting it guide her pace and rhythm.
The gatehouse stood empty; Fulcrum’s guards had already returned to their quarters at the back of the campus. The gate swung shut behind them with a dull metal thump.
She moved her left foot from one rectangle of cement sidewalk to the next, trying to feel each step as solidly as she could, then the right. Then her left again, then the right again. She took a deep breath, filling her lungs completely. Jonah kept his breathing steady, almost silent.
The street was dark but for a few scattered car lights in the distance. They’d crossed the empty drive to reach it; he’d crossed without hesitation, and she followed him. His left foot crossed to the opposite pavement in midstep without breaking rhythm; she did the same, landing on the far side at the same moment that he did. A few cars were parked by the curb; they passed in front of one. It was an SUV with dark tinted windows; no light showed inside and there was no sound. She passed it just a little ahead of Jonah and felt the wind turn and blow her hair out straight from her face as she went.
She walked as rhythmically and solidly as she could. She watched him at the same time, trying to keep their breaths in time, trying not to glance away.
“Can we walk in silence for a while?” he asked after a few seconds. He looked sideways at her as though waiting for an answer.
“Yes.” The word came out on an exhale. “If that’s what you want, yes.”
“I do.” There was the briefest pause, a hesitation as though he expected to be interrupted before continuing: “There’s too much adrenaline in the air right now. It would be better if we just moved and didn’t try to talk about what happened inside.”
Her hands were sweating; she could feel her palms stick to the damp cloth of her slacks with each step. The night was cool enough that her fingers felt cold in the breeze. She still felt too hot inside, as though she might throw up. If she walked faster it might go away, but she kept her steps even because that was what he wanted.
